title: Magnitude and abstinence trajectories of neurocognitive deficits in methamphetamine use disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.statement: In cross-sectional studies, people with a history of regular methamphetamine use, mostly tested within their first months of abstinence, score lower on average than non-using comparison groups on neuropsychological tests: pooled standardized differences of about 0.3 to 0.7 SD for most domains, largest for learning and memory. A meta-analysis restricted to abstinent users found a reliable difference only for learning efficiency (g −0.47), and the largest meta-analysis gives a prediction interval for the overall difference running from a large deficit to a small advantage (−1.58 to 0.22). Users had less education than controls in most studies, and there is evidence of publication bias.
claims.magnitude: Scott et al. (2007; 17 studies, 471 vs 445): d −0.34 (language) to −0.66 (learning). Potvin et al. (2018; 44 studies, 1592 vs 1820): global d 0.46 (95% CI 0.33–0.60) in favour of controls. Basterfield et al. (2019; 31 studies of abstinent users): learning efficiency g −0.47 (−0.58 to −0.37), no reliable difference in fluid reasoning, short-term working memory or reaction speed. Cao et al. (2026; 68 studies, 5244 vs 3801): overall g −0.68 (−0.77 to −0.58), prediction interval −1.58 to 0.22.

claims.statement: Whether test performance improves with abstinence beyond practice effects is not established. In the two studies that retested a control group, users did not improve significantly more than controls over about a month (composite change 0.14 vs 0.00 SD, p=0.33; 18 users, 21 controls) or about a year (group-by-time interaction p=0.13; 25 abstinent users, 58 who kept using, 38 controls); a subgroup of 6 abstinent users impaired at baseline improved more, but so did 6 controls impaired at baseline. Across cross-sectional studies, length of abstinence did not moderate the size of group differences, and few studies tested people abstinent for more than a year.
claims.magnitude: Simon et al. (2010): composite change 0.14 (users) vs 0.00 (controls), t(37)=−1.01, p=0.33; editors' standardized difference in change about 0.32 (95% CI −0.31 to 0.96), so a moderate improvement is not excluded either. Iudicello et al. (2010): all groups improved (time F(1,118)=55.12); group × time p=0.126; abstainer–control gap 3.0 T at baseline, 2.7 T at follow-up. Cao et al. (2026): g −0.70 (<1 month), −0.63 (1–12 months), −0.88 (>12 months; 7 studies), p=0.33.
